passiflora-tripartita.name: Tumbo
passiflora-tripartita.summary: A passionfruit species native to the Andes, known locally as tumbo, poro poro or curuba, grown at high elevations from Peru to Brazil.

canna-indica.name: Achira (Canna indica)
canna-indica.summary: A plant native to the Americas, also called Indian shot or edible canna, grown for its starchy, edible rhizomes.

cusco.name: Cusco
cusco.summary: City in southeastern Peru founded in the 12th century as capital of the Kingdom of Cusco and later the Inca Empire; today a UNESCO World Heritage site and major tourist destination.

escabeche.name: Escabeche
escabeche.summary: A dish found across Spanish, Latin American, and Filipino cuisines of fish, meat, or vegetables marinated or pickled in a vinegar-based sauce.

gast-n-acurio.name: Gastón Acurio
gast-n-acurio.summary: Peruvian chef, born in 1967, credited by a 2022 study with renewing Peruvian cuisine and inspiring a new generation of Peruvian chefs.

viceroyalty-of-peru.name: Viceroyalty of Peru
viceroyalty-of-peru.summary: A Spanish colonial territory created in 1542, governed from Lima, that once covered most of Spanish South America and grew wealthy from silver mined at Potosí.

cusco-school.name: Cusco school
cusco-school.summary: Roman Catholic artistic tradition based in colonial Cusco, Peru, in the 16th to 18th centuries, teaching European techniques and spreading across the Andes to Ecuador and Bolivia.

spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire.name: Spanish conquest of Peru
spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire.summary: The campaign in which Francisco Pizarro's forces captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532, beginning decades of fighting that ended in Spanish victory by 1572.
spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

ngel-arcabucero.name: Ángel arcabucero
ngel-arcabucero.summary: A style of angel imagery showing angels carrying an arquebus instead of a sword, dressed like Criollo and Andean nobles; it arose in Peru in the late 17th century, especially in the Cusco School.

arquebus.name: Arquebus
arquebus.summary: An early long gun that appeared in Europe and the Ottoman Empire in the 15th century, later fitted with a matchlock trigger mechanism.

criollo-people.name: Criollo
criollo-people.summary: A term for people of Spanish descent born in the Americas under Spanish rule, forming a social class below Spanish-born officials; some criollos, like Bolívar and San Martín, later led independence movements.

crown-of-the-andes.name: Crown of the Andes
crown-of-the-andes.summary: A jewelled crown made for a statue of the Virgin Mary in Popayán, Colombia, set with 450 emeralds including the Atahualpa Emerald, said to have been seized from the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532.

popay-n.name: Popayán
popay-n.summary: The capital of Colombia's Cauca department, known for its colonial architecture and as home to seventeen Colombian presidents.

bernardo-bitti.name: Bernardo Bitti
bernardo-bitti.summary: An Italian Jesuit painter (1548–1610) who introduced Mannerism to Peru after arriving in 1575, later regarded as founder of the Cusco School of painting.

mannerism.name: Mannerism
mannerism.summary: A European art style emerging after the Italian High Renaissance around 1520, exaggerating proportion and balance into tension and elegance; it lasted into the late 16th century in Italy.

marcos-zapata.name: Marcos Zapata
marcos-zapata.summary: Peruvian painter (c.1710-1773) of the Cuzco School known for blending Christian subjects with Andean elements, as in his painting The Last Supper featuring local foods.

cusco-cathedral.name: Cathedral of Cusco
cusco-cathedral.summary: Main cathedral of Cusco, Peru, built on the site of an Inca palace and government house and, since 1983, part of the city's UNESCO World Heritage-listed historic center.

andean-baroque.name: Andean Baroque
andean-baroque.summary: An artistic movement in colonial Peru between 1680 and 1780, blending European and indigenous craftsmanship, seen most strikingly in religious architecture.

potos.name: Potosí
potos.summary: A city in Bolivia, among the highest in the world, that grew rapidly after the 1545 discovery of its silver-rich Cerro Rico and became a major source of silver for the Spanish Empire.

luis-de-ria-o.name: Luis de Riaño
luis-de-ria-o.summary: A Peruvian criollo painter (1596-c.1667) of the Cusco School, best known for 1630s frescoes at the Church of San Pedro de Andahuaylillas, nicknamed the 'Sistine Chapel of the Americas.'

angelino-medoro.name: Angelino Medoro
angelino-medoro.summary: Italian painter (1567-1631) active in Latin America whose work in the Viceroyalty of Peru greatly influenced the Cuzco School art movement.

andahuaylillas-district.name: Andahuaylillas
andahuaylillas-district.summary: A district and town in Peru's Quispicanchi Province, about 45 km south of Cusco, known as one of the main stops on the Andean Baroque Route.

quechua-people.name: Quechua people
quechua-people.summary: Indigenous peoples of South America, native mainly to Peru, who speak Quechuan languages; the Incas of Cusco began as one such group before expanding.

calamarca.name: Church of Calamarca
calamarca.summary: A late 16th-century church in Bolivia holding the largest surviving collection of colonial 'angel arquebusier' paintings.

master-of-calamarca.name: Master of Calamarca
master-of-calamarca.summary: A name for an anonymous 18th-century Bolivian artist, possibly José López de los Ríos, who painted the angel series in the Calamarca church near La Paz.

atahualpa.name: Atahualpa
atahualpa.summary: Last effective Inca emperor, reigning from April 1532 until his capture and execution the following year during the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire.

francisco-pizarro.name: Francisco Pizarro
francisco-pizarro.summary: Spanish conquistador (c. 1478–1541) who led the conquest of the Inca Empire, capturing and executing Emperor Atahualpa and founding Lima in 1535.

jacob-de-gheyn-ii.name: Jacob de Gheyn II
jacob-de-gheyn-ii.summary: Dutch painter and engraver (c. 1565–1629) whose work marks the shift from Northern Mannerism to Dutch realism.

inca-civil-war.name: Inca Civil War
inca-civil-war.summary: War fought from 1529 to 1532 between half-brothers Huáscar and Atahualpa over succession to the Inca throne, weakening the empire ahead of the Spanish conquest.

t-pac-amaru-ii.name: Túpac Amaru II
t-pac-amaru-ii.summary: Indigenous cacique (about 1742–1781) who led a major rebellion against Spanish rule in Peru and was later elevated to a symbolic figure in the fight for independence and indigenous rights.

gonzalo-jim-nez-de-quesada.name: Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada
gonzalo-jim-nez-de-quesada.summary: Spanish explorer and conquistador (1509–1579) who conquered territory in what is now Colombia, founded Bogotá, and later searched unsuccessfully for El Dorado.

muisca.name: Muisca
muisca.summary: Pre-Columbian culture and colonial-era communities of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense in Colombia, also called the Chibcha, whose traditions lasted into the early 19th century.

bourbon-reforms.name: Bourbon Reforms
bourbon-reforms.summary: A series of 18th-century political and economic changes by the Spanish Crown under the House of Bourbon, aiming to modernize Spain and make its American colonies more efficient and profitable.

francisco-de-toledo.name: Francisco de Toledo
francisco-de-toledo.summary: Spanish aristocrat (1515–1582), fifth Viceroy of Peru, who organized the viceroyalty, forcibly relocated many indigenous Andeans into new settlements, and had the last Inca ruler executed.

vilcabamba-peru.name: Vilcabamba
vilcabamba-peru.summary: The last refuge of the Inca Empire, serving as capital of the Neo-Inca State from 1539 until its fall to the Spanish in 1572; its ruins were later rediscovered and confirmed as Vilcabamba in the 20th century.

t-pac-amaru.name: Túpac Amaru
t-pac-amaru.summary: Last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State (1545–1572), executed by the Spanish after a months-long pursuit following the fall of the last independent Inca stronghold.

juan-santos-atahualpa.name: Juan Santos Atahualpa
juan-santos-atahualpa.summary: The messianic leader of an indigenous rebellion, begun in 1742, in the Amazon Basin against Spanish rule in Peru, who claimed to be the reincarnation of the Inca emperor Atahualpa.

tarma-province.name: Tarma
tarma-province.summary: A Peruvian province in the Andean Junín Region, positioned between the highlands and the high forest.

jauja-province.name: Jauja Province
jauja-province.summary: A Peruvian province in the Junín Region whose capital city, Jauja, was founded by Francisco Pizarro as the first capital of Peru, on the site of the earlier Inca-era center Hatun Xauxa.

panche-people.name: Panche
panche-people.summary: An indigenous people who lived in what is now Colombia, numbering more than 30,000 at the time of the Spanish conquest.

battle-of-tocarema.name: Battle of Tocarema
battle-of-tocarema.summary: A battle fought on 19 to 20 August 1538 in Colombia in which Spanish conquistadors under Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada, allied with the Muisca zipa Sagipa, defeated the indigenous Panche people.

sagipa.name: Sagipa
sagipa.summary: The fifth and last ruler of Muyquytá (now Bogotá), from 1537 until his death in 1539, seen by some Muisca as a usurper of his nephew's rightful claim.

tisquesusa.name: Tisquesusa
tisquesusa.summary: Fourth and last independent ruler of the southern Muisca confederation in what is now Colombia, who died in 1537 at Facatativá during the Spanish conquest; the Spanish pronunciation of his name gave rise to the city name Bogotá.

juan-de-sanct-mart-n.name: Juan de Sanct Martín
juan-de-sanct-mart-n.summary: A Spanish conquistador who took part in the expedition into the Colombian Andes led by Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada and founded Cuítiva, Boyacá, in 1550.

juan-de-c-spedes-ruiz.name: Juan de Céspedes
juan-de-c-spedes-ruiz.summary: Spanish conquistador (1501 or 1505 – 1573 or 1576) who arrived in the Americas in 1521, founded the town of Pasca near Bogotá, and later served as mayor of Bogotá and lieutenant general of colonial New Granada.

pedro-sim-n.name: Pedro Simón
pedro-sim-n.summary: Spanish Franciscan friar and chronicler (1574–c. 1628) of the indigenous peoples of what is now Colombia and Venezuela, an important source for Muisca scholarship.

felipe-guaman-poma-de-ayala.name: Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala
felipe-guaman-poma-de-ayala.summary: Quechua nobleman (c. 1535–after 1616) who chronicled and denounced Spanish mistreatment of Andean natives in his illustrated chronicle El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno.

philip-iii-of-spain.name: Philip III of Spain
philip-iii-of-spain.summary: King of Spain and Portugal from 1598 to 1621, whose reign brought relative peace to Western Europe though power was mostly delegated to his chief minister, the Duke of Lerma.

titu-cusi.name: Titu Cusi
titu-cusi.summary: Inca ruler of Vilcabamba from 1563 to 1571, son of Manco Inca Yupanqui, who wrote a rare 1570 account of the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire from an Inca elite's viewpoint.

francisco-xerez.name: Francisco Xerez
francisco-xerez.summary: Spanish explorer turned historian (1495–1565?), personal secretary to Pizarro during the conquest of Peru, who wrote a detailed account of the campaign.

pedro-s-nchez-de-la-hoz.name: Pedro Sánchez de la Hoz
pedro-s-nchez-de-la-hoz.summary: Spanish conquistador (1514–1547) who served as secretary to Pizarro in Peru, wrote an early account of the conquest, and later obtained land grants south of the Strait of Magellan.

classical-quechua.name: Classical Quechua
classical-quechua.summary: Name for two historical forms of Quechua: the lingua franca of the Inca Empire (1438 to 1533), and the written form used for religious and administrative purposes in the Spanish-ruled Andes, mostly from the late 16th to mid-17th century.

pedro-cieza-de-le-n.name: Pedro Cieza de León
pedro-cieza-de-le-n.summary: Spanish conquistador and chronicler (c. 1518–1554) whose Crónicas del Perú is considered fundamental to understanding Inca history and the empire's structure.

huarochir-manuscript.name: Huarochirí Manuscript
huarochir-manuscript.summary: A late-16th-century Quechua text recording myths and religious traditions of the Huarochirí region, described as 'the closest thing to an Andean bible'.

jos-mar-a-arguedas.name: José María Arguedas
jos-mar-a-arguedas.summary: Peruvian novelist, poet, and anthropologist (1911–1969) fluent in Quechua, celebrated for his intimate portrayals of Indigenous Andean culture blending Spanish and Quechua.

royal-danish-library.name: Royal Danish Library
royal-danish-library.summary: Denmark's national library, formed in 2017 by merging the State and University Library in Aarhus with the former Royal Library in Copenhagen, still maintaining both locations.

paul-rivet.name: Paul Rivet
paul-rivet.summary: French ethnologist (1876–1958) who founded the Musée de l'Homme in 1937 and theorized that South America was partly populated by migrants from Australia and Melanesia.

juan-de-santa-cruz-pachacuti-yamqui-salc.name: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui Salcamaygua
juan-de-santa-cruz-pachacuti-yamqui-salc.summary: An indigenous Peruvian chronicler of the late 16th–17th century, author of a short but historically valuable account of the antiquities of the Kingdom of Peru.
juan-de-santa-cruz-pachacuti-yamqui-salc.source_title: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui Salcamaygua

francisco-de-vila.name: Francisco de Ávila
francisco-de-vila.summary: Peruvian priest and theologian (c. 1573–1647) who led campaigns against indigenous idolatry and commissioned the Huarochirí Manuscript, the key source on Inca mythology and Andean religion.

gaspar-de-guzm-n-count-duke-of-olivares.name: Count-Duke of Olivares
gaspar-de-guzm-n-count-duke-of-olivares.summary: Spanish royal favourite and chief minister to Philip IV (1587–1645) whose foreign wars and centralizing reforms overextended Spain and provoked revolts, leading to his downfall.
gaspar-de-guzm-n-count-duke-of-olivares.source_title: Gaspar de Guzmán, Count-Duke of Olivares

cornelius-pedersen-lerche.name: Cornelius Pedersen Lerche
cornelius-pedersen-lerche.summary: Danish nobleman (1615-1681) who served as Denmark's envoy to the Spanish court.

cerro-rico.name: Cerro Rico
cerro-rico.summary: A mountain near Potosí, Bolivia, popularly seen as 'made of' silver, that supplied vast quantities of it to the Spanish Empire and is estimated to have produced 85% of central Andean silver.

patio-process.name: Patio process
patio-process.summary: A method using mercury amalgamation to extract silver from ore, first used at scale by Bartolomé de Medina in Mexico in 1554, replacing smelting in Spanish colonies.

cinchona.name: Cinchona
cinchona.summary: A genus of Andean trees whose bark yields quinine, the main effective treatment for malaria during European colonialism until synthetic quinine appeared in 1944.

alvaro-alonso-barba.name: Alvaro Alonso Barba
alvaro-alonso-barba.summary: A Catholic priest and metallurgist born in Spain in 1569 who lived at Potosí and in 1609 invented the pan amalgamation process for extracting silver with mercury.

pan-amalgamation.name: Pan process
pan-amalgamation.summary: A faster method for extracting silver from ore, invented by Alvaro Alonso Barba in 1609 in Potosí, mixing ore with salt and mercury in shallow copper pans.

huancavelica.name: Huancavelica
huancavelica.summary: A Peruvian city founded in 1572, capital of the Huancavelica department, high in the Andes and long one of the poorest cities in Peru.

jer-nimo-luis-de-cabrera.name: Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera
jer-nimo-luis-de-cabrera.summary: A Spanish conquistador (1528–1574), early colonial governor of what is now northwestern Argentina, and founder of the city of Córdoba.

almad-n.name: Almadén
almad-n.summary: Spanish town whose mercury deposits produced roughly 250,000 metric tons of mercury over 2,000 years, the largest such source in the world.

pallaqueo.name: Pallaqueo
pallaqueo.summary: The hand selection of ore-bearing rock fragments in Andean mining, historically practiced at sites like Potosí and sometimes legalized as a form of scavenging that boosted output.

battle-of-cajamarca.name: Battle of Cajamarca
battle-of-cajamarca.summary: The 1532 ambush in which a small Spanish force under Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa, killing thousands of his unarmed attendants and opening the conquest of Peru.

sapa-inca.name: Sapa Inca
sapa-inca.summary: The Quechua title for the Inca Empire's supreme monarch, believed to be the sun god's son, a hereditary position held from around 1100 CE until Atahualpa's execution in 1533.

tom-s-katari.name: Tomás Katari
tom-s-katari.summary: Aymara peasant and local chief in northern Potosí who led an uprising in Upper Peru, in present-day Bolivia, in the late 18th century, dying in 1781.

t-pac-katari.name: Túpac Katari
t-pac-katari.summary: Aymara leader (about 1750–1781) who led a major rebellion in colonial Upper Peru, besieging La Paz for six months before being captured and executed.

manco-inca-yupanqui.name: Manco Inca Yupanqui
manco-inca-yupanqui.summary: A son of Huayna Cápac who was installed as a puppet Inca emperor by the Spanish before founding the independent Neo-Inca State at Vilcabamba; he lived from about 1515 to 1544.

neo-inca-state.name: Neo-Inca State
neo-inca-state.summary: A rump Inca state founded in 1537 at Vilcabamba by Manco Inca Yupanqui after the Spanish conquest, lasting until 1572 when its last ruler, Túpac Amaru, was captured and executed.

cacique.name: Cacique
cacique.summary: A Spanish-derived term for a tribal chieftain among Indigenous Caribbean and Latin American peoples, later used broadly by colonial administrators for any Indigenous leader.

kuraka.name: Kuraka
kuraka.summary: Title for a governor or communal authority in Andean civilizations and the Inca Empire, who collected taxes, held religious authority, and mediated between local ayllus and the Sapa Inca.

mit-a.name: Mit'a
mit-a.summary: A system of mandatory labor service in the Inca Empire, later reused by Spain to draft workers for mines; citizens owed a set number of days each year to the state.

huarochir-province.name: Huarochirí
huarochir-province.summary: A province in Peru's Lima department, whose capital is Matucana.

real-audiencia-of-lima.name: Real Audiencia of Lima
real-audiencia-of-lima.summary: A superior royal court in the Viceroyalty of Peru, created in 1542 and based in Lima, with jurisdiction over most of Spanish-ruled South America until it ceased functioning in 1821.

governorate-of-new-castile.name: New Castile
governorate-of-new-castile.summary: The Spanish colonial territory, roughly covering modern Peru, granted to Francisco Pizarro as governor by King Charles I in 1529 following the conquest of the Inca Empire.

ubaque.name: Ubaque
ubaque.summary: A municipality and town in Colombia's Cundinamarca department, about 56 km from Bogotá.

ch-a-goddess.name: Chía (goddess)
ch-a-goddess.summary: A triple lunar deity central to the Muisca religion of pre-Columbian Colombia, worshipped as patron of the Zipa ruler and paired as wife to the sun god Sué.

muisca-religion.name: Sué
muisca-religion.summary: Muisca god of the Sun, husband of the moon goddess Chía, their pairing representing the complementary nature of man and woman and the sacredness of marriage.

peter-gow-anthropologist.name: Peter Gow
peter-gow-anthropologist.summary: Social anthropologist (1958–2021) renowned for his work on Amazonia, who taught at the University of St Andrews.

ayahuasca.name: Ayahuasca
ayahuasca.summary: A psychoactive brew made from an Amazonian vine, used by Indigenous peoples for spiritual and medicinal purposes since at least the 17th century.

icaro.name: Ícaros
icaro.summary: A South American term for a magic song, used especially for the medicine songs maestros perform in ayahuasca ceremonies among Amazonian peoples.

quechuan-languages.name: Quechua language
quechuan-languages.summary: Indigenous language family that originated in central Peru and spread through the Andes, the most widely spoken pre-Columbian language family in the Americas and the primary language of the Inca Empire.

chiminigagua.name: Chiminigagua
chiminigagua.summary: The supreme being and creator god in the religion of the Muisca, one of the four advanced pre-Columbian civilizations, who lived on the Andean Altiplano Cundiboyacense.

lake-guatavita.name: Lake Guatavita
lake-guatavita.summary: A circular lake in the Colombian Andes tied to Muisca gold rituals, famous as the inspiration for the legend of El Dorado.

siecha-lakes.name: Siecha Lakes
siecha-lakes.summary: Three glacial lakes in Colombia's Chingaza park, considered sacred by the Muisca people before the Spanish conquest of the 1530s.

ch-a-cundinamarca.name: Chía, Cundinamarca
ch-a-cundinamarca.summary: A city near Bogotá, Colombia, with pre-Columbian origins, today known for its restaurants and its university.

chachapoya-culture.name: Chachapoya
chachapoya-culture.summary: An Andean people called the 'Warriors of the Clouds' who lived in Peru's cloud forests, resisting Inca conquest before being absorbed into the Inca Empire shortly before the Spanish arrived.

chaqu-n.name: Chaquén
chaqu-n.summary: The Muisca god of sports and fertility, believed to have trained the guecha warriors who resisted the Spanish conquest.

tejo-sport.name: Tejo
tejo-sport.summary: A traditional Colombian throwing sport, also called turmequé, distinctive for small targets packed with gunpowder that explode on impact.
